clue.text: Making no progress in set problem

blocks.note: first meaning: standing still, unchanging
second meaning: crackling interference on a radio or television set

explanation.walkthrough: 'Set problem' reads like a maths exercise, but the set is a TV or radio, and its problem is crackle on the reception.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalled situation is described as static, and the same word names electrical interference heard as hiss on a receiver.

clue.text: Players hoping for a full house from pack, say?

definitions.text: Players hoping for a full house

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the word and take another word that is pronounced identically

blocks.clueFragment: Players hoping for a full house
blocks.note: a company of actors wanting a sold-out theatre
a pack, such as of Scouts or Brownies, is a troop

explanation.surface: Card players with a pack, hoping to draw a full house in poker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players', 'full house' and 'pack' all suggest a card game; the players are actors and the full house is a packed theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A troupe is a touring company of performers, who want every seat in the house filled.

clue.text: Element found in West when in short supply

definitions.text: Element found in West when in short supply

blocks.clueFragment: Element found in West when in short supply
blocks.note: surface reading: some substance that turns up in the West at times of scarcity
setter's reading: West in short form is W, the chemical symbol of a metallic element

explanation.surface: A scarce mineral discovered out West during a shortage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short supply' sounds like scarcity, but 'in short' means abbreviated: West shortened is W, the symbol of this element.
explanation.definitionFit: The metal with symbol W is a chemical element, whose symbol comes from its other name, wolfram.

clue.text: Crooked fence, perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: dishonest, unlawful
second meaning: a fence, a receiver of stolen goods, is one kind of lawbreaker

explanation.walkthrough: 'Crooked fence' paints a bent garden fence; in slang a fence handles stolen goods, so 'perhaps' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works as an adjective for anything unlawful and as a noun for any lawbreaker, of which a fence is one type.

clue.text: Daub page in a couple of seconds

indicators.note: in places the page inside the other words, which wrap around it

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for seconds
P is the abbreviation for page
of a couple, the second is the latter

explanation.surface: Someone smears a page of paint in a blur, all over in a couple of seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A couple of seconds' is split: one second is S, the other is the second of a pair, LATTER. The page goes inside: S(P)LATTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To daub is to smear paint or mud carelessly, which is what splattering a surface amounts to.

clue.text: A High Church point of view?

definitions.text: A High Church point of view?

blocks.clueFragment: A High Church point of view?
blocks.note: surface reading: an opinion held by Anglo-Catholic churchgoers
setter's reading: a tall pointed structure on top of a church, seen from afar

explanation.surface: Asking what the Anglo-Catholic wing of the church thinks.
explanation.walkthrough: High Church is a tradition within Anglicanism; read literally it is a church that is high, and its point is the tall spire, something you view.
explanation.definitionFit: A church's tower topped with a spire rises to a point high above the building, visible for miles.

clue.text: Championship point wasted following disturbance

indicators.note: wasted means ruined, so the word point is broken up and its letters rearranged
following places the reworked word after the other piece

blocks.note: ado is fuss or commotion
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tennis player throws away championship point after a disturbance in the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Championship point' is the tennis phrase; here championship means championing a cause, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Championship of a cause means taking it up and backing it, which is the same as its adoption.

clue.text: Two sorts of wrong topping on a pancake

indicators.note: in a down entry, topping means sitting above, so these pieces come before the next one

blocks.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law
an ill is a harm or wrong
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook puts two kinds of wrong topping on a pancake.
explanation.walkthrough: A tort is a civil wrong in law, and an ill is a harm; both sit on top of A in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A tortilla is a thin flat Mexican bread made from maize or wheat, which is pancake-like.

clue.text: Sort of football played in school match

blocks.note: Rugby is an English public school
a match, such as a marriage, is a union

explanation.surface: A sort of football played in a school match.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby School, a private school in Warwickshire, gave its name to the game. Match here is a marriage, not a fixture.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugby union is the fifteen-a-side code of rugby football, one kind of football.

clue.text: County's season not a productive period

blocks.note: Down is a county of Northern Ireland
a season is a time, as in 'the time of year'

explanation.surface: A county's off-season, when farms or tourism produce little.
explanation.walkthrough: Down is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Downtime is the interval when machines or workers are idle, so nothing gets made.

clue.text: Despicable type conclusively no great shakes?

indicators.note: conclusively points at the end of the word no, keeping only its final letter
shaking the word great jumbles its letters into a new order

blocks.note: the last letter of no
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sneering verdict that some contemptible person is, in the end, no great shakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No great shakes' is an idiom for unimpressive, which hides that shakes is the anagram signal. TOERAG is British slang for a worthless, contemptible person.
explanation.definitionFit: Toerag is a British insult for a scoundrel or lowlife, someone held in contempt.

clue.text: Decorate wings of priory, bringing back more appropriate interior

indicators.note: the wings of a building are its two ends, so only the outer letters of priory are used
bringing something back returns it the way it came, so the word is written right to left
interior means the inside, so this piece sits between the two outer letters

blocks.note: the first and last letters of priory
fitter means more suitable or more appropriate

explanation.surface: Restoring a priory, with the wings brought back to a more fitting interior design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bringing back' sounds like restoring the building, but it tells you to read the word for more appropriate backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To prettify is to make something look pretty, which is to adorn or decorate it.

clue.text: Sort of tennis the Spanish watch

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant form of it, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Spaniards watching some form of tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' looks like a verb for the Spanish spectators, but it is the noun: a guard on watch.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentinel is a guard or lookout, someone keeping watch; a watch can also mean such a sentry.

clue.text: Can drug, say, become such a sweet substance?

indicators.note: to become is to turn into something else, so the letters are rearranged into another form

blocks.note: the letters of can, drug and say together

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a drug could be turned into a sweet treat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example', but its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Sugar candy is crystallised sugar, a confection eaten as a sweet.

clue.text: Very small measure of coffee or large 'un, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the words could be arranged otherwise, so their letters are reordered

blocks.note: the letters of large and un together

explanation.surface: A coffee order: a tiny cup, or perhaps a large one instead.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'small or large' choice sounds like cup sizes; it is really a contrast between a grain of instant coffee and the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Instant coffee comes as granules, each one a tiny grain of the product.

clue.text: Trusted friend to change self-image

blocks.note: to alter is to change
the ego is one's sense of self

explanation.surface: A trusted friend urges someone to change how they see themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is Latin for 'other self'.
explanation.definitionFit: An alter ego can mean an intimate and trusted friend, someone so close they are like a second self.

clue.text: It's not usually fair for this to be put up

definitions.text: It's not usually fair for this to be put up

blocks.clueFragment: It's not usually fair for this to be put up
blocks.note: surface reading: something it is generally unjust to make someone tolerate
setter's reading: the weather is seldom fine when this is raised over your head

explanation.surface: A complaint that someone shouldn't have to put up with something unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: Fair means just in the surface, but here it means fine, dry weather; put up means opened over your head, not tolerated.
explanation.definitionFit: A rain shield on a folding frame is opened when it rains, so the weather is rarely fine at the time.

clue.text: Belgian flying from part of India

indicators.note: something flying is tossed through the air, so its letters land in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Belgian flying in from somewhere in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From part of India' looks like the flight's origin; it is the definition, an adjective of place.
explanation.definitionFit: Bengal is a region of the Indian subcontinent, and Bengali describes a person or thing coming from there.

clue.text: Scene that has none of the actors in

definitions.text: Scene that has none of the actors in

blocks.clueFragment: Scene that has none of the actors in
blocks.note: surface reading: a part of a play in which no cast members appear
setter's reading: a film scene shot outdoors, with the actors not inside a building

explanation.surface: A curious scene in a play with no cast on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'None of the actors in' sounds like an empty cast; it means the actors are out of doors, the film term for an outdoor shot.
explanation.definitionFit: In film-making, the word names an outdoor shot or set, as opposed to an interior one.

clue.text: Film star bound to go to the wall

blocks.note: Clark Gable was a Hollywood film star
a bound is a limit, an end

explanation.surface: A film star doomed to go to the wall, to fail and be ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go to the wall' is an idiom for being ruined; here 'to go to' joins pieces to their definition, 'the wall'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gable end is the triangular-topped end wall of a building with a pitched roof.

clue.text: Queen captured in crazy attack

indicators.note: something captured is held inside its captor, so it goes within the other word

blocks.note: batty means mad
ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the Queen

explanation.surface: The Queen taken prisoner during a mad assault.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, for Elizabeth Regina, is the standard crossword Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, battery is the unlawful use of force against a person, an assault or attack.

clue.text: Endlessly hang about after breakdown driving here in Austria

indicators.note: without its end, the word hang loses its final letter
a breakdown breaks something into pieces that are put back together differently

blocks.note: hang without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A motorist stranded on a road in Austria, endlessly hanging about after the car broke down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driving here in Austria' is the definition: where you would drive, a motorway in a German-speaking country.
explanation.definitionFit: An Autobahn is a motorway in Germany or Austria, the road you would be driving on there.

clue.text: Doubled up laughing about new Conservative leader

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the laughter wraps round the other letters

blocks.note: a laugh, ho, written twice
N is the abbreviation for new
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: Someone doubled up with laughter at the new Tory leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doubled up' reads as bent over laughing, but it means the laugh is written twice: HO(N C)HO.
explanation.definitionFit: A honcho is informal American slang, from Japanese, for a boss or person in charge.

clue.text: Sweep — cricket stroke that's straightforward

blocks.note: to sweep a table is to clear it
the cut is a cricket shot played square on the off side

explanation.surface: A commentator calls a cricket sweep shot simple and obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: The sweep is itself a cricket shot, which makes 'Sweep' look like part of the cricket picture; here it means clear. The cut is a shot played across the line to the off side.
explanation.definitionFit: Clear-cut means plain and unambiguous, with no room for doubt, which is straightforward.

clue.text: Intense anger uncalled for, with seconds out

indicators.note: out means removed, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: uncalled for means unnecessary, needless
S is short for second, so seconds is two of them

explanation.surface: A boxing match where fury is out of place, and the seconds are ordered from the ring.
explanation.walkthrough: Seconds are a boxer's corner men, which fits the fight picture; here they are just two S's removed from NEEDLESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Needle is British slang for hostility or bad blood, as in a needle match between bitter rivals.

clue.text: Late news swamped by distant crisis

indicators.note: something swamped is engulfed and surrounded, so it sits inside the other word

blocks.note: late can mean former, ex
an icy, distant manner is cold and aloof
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Late-breaking news from far away is lost in the confusion of a crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late news' reads as a bulletin, but late means former, as in the late chairman, and gen is British slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: An exigency is an urgent need or pressing emergency, which amounts to a crisis.

clue.text: Home Guard the old, old soldier trains with?

blocks.note: ye is the archaic spelling of the
O is a standard abbreviation for old
a soldier in the ranks is a man
RY is the abbreviation for railway, which carries trains

explanation.surface: An old soldier who drills with Britain's wartime Home Guard volunteers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Guard was Britain's Second World War volunteer defence force. The question mark signals the definition is loose: the yeomanry was an earlier volunteer cavalry for home defence.
explanation.definitionFit: The yeomanry were volunteer cavalry regiments raised to defend Britain at home, a home-defence force like the Home Guard.

clue.text: Excited socialist given roasting

blocks.note: red is a common label for a socialist
roasting means very hot

explanation.surface: A left-wing firebrand worked up after being roasted by critics.
explanation.walkthrough: A roasting looks like a telling-off; here it is just heat.
explanation.definitionFit: Red-hot can describe passions or people running at a high pitch of excitement or fervour.
